description: Brassbuckle's first-year lecture is the one every child in Kettleport could give. Three hundred and twelve years ago the sea began to boil; the city still calls it the Scald. Seven engineers built the Great Kettle, the boiler at the city's heart, and rode its steam into the sky with the town bolted on. That day is the Lift. Their heirs, the Board of Gauges, have kept the city rising since. She gives it well, with slides, and ends on the Lift itself, the painting that hangs in every schoolroom. At the end she asks for questions, in the voice of a woman who would prefer there were none.

options.label: Take careful notes, and ask a good question about the Great Kettle's valves.

success.text: It is a very good question, and Brassbuckle answers it for twenty minutes, with diagrams, in a way that makes the whole room late for dinner. Afterwards she lends you her own notes on the Kettle's valve gear. They are in three colours of ink and better than any book in the library.

options.label: Ask how far the Scald has climbed since the Lift.

success.text: The lecture hall goes quiet, the way a room does when someone says a thing out loud that everyone has thought. "Further than it did," says Brassbuckle, "and never as far as the Kettle can climb. That is the whole of engineering, and the whole of this course." Several students look at you on the way out. One of them nods.
